clinicalPearls: A birth-related brachial plexus injury affecting the upper roots (C5-C6, sometimes C7)
The affected arm lies adducted and internally rotated with the forearm pronated and wrist flexed, the classic waiter's tip posture
The Moro reflex is asymmetric, but grasp is preserved because the lower roots are spared
Risk factors include shoulder dystocia, macrosomia, instrumental delivery and breech birth
An intact grasp helps distinguish it from lower plexus (Klumpke) palsy, and Horner syndrome suggests a more severe root avulsion
Most cases recover with early physiotherapy; persistent deficit at a few months warrants specialist referral for possible surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Erb's palsy results from traction on the upper brachial plexus during delivery, typically when the shoulder is depressed as the head is delivered, as in shoulder dystocia. Stretching injures the C5-C6 (and sometimes C7) nerve roots, ranging from neurapraxia to rupture or root avulsion. The upper-root distribution explains the weakness of shoulder abduction and external rotation, elbow flexion and forearm supination, producing the characteristic posture, while preserved lower roots maintain hand function. The severity of the nerve injury determines the potential for recovery.
additionalDifferentials: Clavicular or humeral fracture causing pseudoparalysis
Osteomyelitis or septic arthritis of the shoulder (as a cause of a still arm)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination of the posture, active movement and reflexes
Assessment for Horner syndrome suggesting root avulsion
Radiographs to exclude clavicular or humeral fracture
Neurophysiology and MRI in persistent or severe cases
redFlags: Horner syndrome or a flail arm suggesting severe avulsion or total plexus injury
Respiratory distress suggesting phrenic nerve involvement
No recovery of biceps function by a few months of age
reference.prognosis: The majority of infants recover spontaneously or with physiotherapy over weeks to months; a minority with severe injury have persistent weakness and may benefit from nerve or later orthopaedic surgery.
pitfalls: Missing an associated fracture causing pseudoparalysis
Overlooking Horner syndrome as a marker of severe injury
Failing to refer non-recovering cases in time for surgical options
Neglecting early physiotherapy and joint contracture prevention
